title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 14: The Power of the Supreme Court to Review Internal Acts of Congress
keywords: The Power of the Supreme Court to Review Internal Acts of Congress
primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's explanation, from his own ponencia in Santiago v. Guingona, that the Supreme Court does have jurisdiction to review internal acts of the Senate whenever a petition alleges a violation of the Constitution or grave abuse of discretion, even though it dismissed that petition on the merits

The doctrinal distinction at the heart of the chapter: jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the petition, so the Court may take a case and then find no violation -- which is different from holding that it may never look into the internal affairs of a coequal branch

The Senate leadership dispute that produced the ruling: Fernan's election as Senate President 20 to 2, Tatad's claim to the minority leadership, Fernan's recognition of Guingona on the strength of seven Lakas-NUCD-UMDP senators, and the quo warranto petition of Santiago and Tatad under Article VI, Section 16 (1)

The internal debate among the Justices: Mendoza's position that the question was political and beyond jurisdiction, Vitug's plea for judicial statesmanship rather than judicial tyranny, Romero's fealty to her Arroyo and Tolentino positions, and CJP's answer that adopting Mendoza's view would signal that the Court will never review legislative acts however grave the alleged violation
sub_topics: He opens with the Court's role as the arm vested with the ultimate power and duty to interpret the Constitution, the guardian of the Constitution and the conscience of society

He states the two and only two grounds on which the Court will strike down acts of the political departments -- unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion -- and disclaims any review of their wisdom, merit or propriety

He poses the chapter's question: whether the Court may review internal acts of the Senate on an allegation that they contravened the Constitution, and answers with Santiago v. Guingona's affirmative ruling

He grounds that answer in the settled doctrine that jurisdiction over the subject matter is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition, regardless of whether the petitioner is entitled to the relief sought

He recounts the facts: on July 27, 1998 the Senate elected Marcelo B. Fernan its President by 20 to 2; Tatad, the losing candidate, with Santiago's agreement declared himself minority leader; on July 30 Fernan, acting on a letter of seven Lakas-NUCD-UMDP senators, recognized Teofisto T. Guingona Jr. instead

He lays out the petitioners' theory that 'majority' means those who voted for the winning Senate President and took committee chairmanships, so that only the remainder could choose a minority leader and Guingona, a Fernan voter, could not qualify

He notes the Court's unanimous denial of the petition: absent a showing of constitutional violation or grave abuse, constitutional respect for a coequal branch bars the Court from prying into the Senate's internal workings
He affirms the Constitution's grant to each house of the power to determine the rules of its proceedings, an exclusive realm in which the legislature is supreme

He restates his ponencia's merits holding that Fernan and Guingona acted within the confines of their positions, so no grave abuse could be imputed where no constitutional, statutory or Senate rule was shown to have been violated

He presents the countervailing view of Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, joined by two others, that the petition should have been dismissed for want of jurisdiction because the composition of the Senate minority is a political question addressed solely to that body
He quotes Mendoza's Marbury v. Madison analogy that a court doing a Marbury has no jurisdiction except to declare itself without jurisdiction

He answers that jurisdiction is fixed by the allegations, not by the respondents' arguments or by the Court's later finding of no merit, and that once acquired it is not lost because the petition fails
He reads the constitutional phrase 'any branch or instrumentality of the government' as including the two houses of Congress, so the duty to check grave abuse reaches them

He concedes the limit: where the allegations show neither a prima facie constitutional violation nor grave abuse but only a breach of internal rules, the Court may dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, exactly as Mendoza described

He quotes Justice Jose C. Vitug's Separate Opinion that judicial power still succumbs to separation of powers, that grave abuse has no hornbook definition, and that only a clear disregard of a specific constitutional precept can unbolt the steel door for judicial intervention

He quotes Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero's Separate Opinion recalling Arroyo v. De Venecia -- Joker Arroyo's challenge to the passage of the sin-taxes law, RA 8240 -- and her insistence that she had not abandoned her Tolentino position because the rules there violated were purely internal

He observes that neither Vitug nor Romero discussed jurisdiction, and closes by warning that had the majority followed Mendoza, the Court would have signaled that it will never pass upon internal legislative acts, however serious the allegations

stances.claim: The Court has jurisdiction to inquire into internal acts of the Senate whenever a petition contains prima facie allegations that the Constitution was violated or that discretion was gravely abused, because jurisdiction is fixed by the allegations and is not lost when the petition is later found meritless.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural first principles applied to a constitutional question: separating the taking of jurisdiction from the disposition on the merits

stances.claim: The constitutional phrase 'any branch or instrumentality of the government' includes both houses of Congress, so the judiciary's duty to check grave abuse extends to legislative action.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual reading of the expanded certiorari clause, stated as his own understanding

stances.claim: On the merits the petition rightly failed, since each house determines the rules of its own proceedings and no provision of the Constitution, the laws or the Rules of the Senate was shown to have been violated by Fernan or Guingona.
stances.rhetorical_move: deference on the merits paired with firmness on jurisdiction -- constitutional respect for a coequal branch rather than a jurisdictional bar

stances.claim: Justice Mendoza's position that the question was purely political and beyond the Court's jurisdiction would, if adopted, have signaled that the Court will never review internal legislative acts even when a petition seriously alleges constitutional violations.
stances.rhetorical_move: consequence argument against a colleague's rule, conceding it applies only where the allegations show nothing beyond a breach of internal rules

notable_anecdotes: He recalls the Senate leadership fight of July 1998, when Tatad, having lost 20 to 2 with only Miriam Defensor Santiago beside him, declared himself minority leader and was displaced by Guingona on the strength of a letter from seven Lakas-NUCD-UMDP senators.
He quotes his own ponencia's line that constitutional respect for a coequal branch prevents the Court from prying into the internal workings of the Senate.
He reproduces Justice Mendoza's Marbury v. Madison formulation that a court doing a Marbury has no jurisdiction except to declare itself without jurisdiction.

He quotes Justice Vitug's warning that grave abuse is 'clearly too relative a phrase to be its own sentinel against misuse' and that the Constitution institutionalized judicial statesmanship, not judicial tyranny.
He notes Justice Romero's pointed clarification that concurring in Arroyo v. De Venecia, the sin-taxes case brought by Joker Arroyo, did not mean abandoning her earlier Tolentino position.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' used CJP's own ponencia in Santiago v. Guingona to explain when the Supreme Court may look into the internal acts of Congress. He began with the Court's role as guardian of the Constitution and conscience of society, and with the limit on that role: it will strike down acts of the political departments only for unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion, never for want of wisdom or propriety. The case arose when the Senate elected Marcelo B. Fernan its President on July 27, 1998 by a vote of 20 to 2, Senator Francisco S. Tatad, the losing nominee supported only by Senator Miriam Defensor Santiago, claimed the minority leadership, and Fernan instead recognized Teofisto T. Guingona Jr. on the strength of a letter from seven Lakas-NUCD-UMDP senators. Santiago and Tatad sued in quo warranto, arguing that Article VI, Section 16 (1) required the Court to define 'majority' and 'minority' and that Guingona, having voted for Fernan, could not lead the minority. The Court unanimously denied the petition, holding that absent any showing of a constitutional violation or grave abuse, constitutional respect for a coequal branch forbade prying into the Senate's internal workings, and that Fernan and Guingona had acted within their competence. Three Justices led by Vicente V. Mendoza would have dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, calling the composition of the Senate minority a political question and invoking Marbury v. Madison for the proposition that such a court has no jurisdiction except to declare itself without jurisdiction. CJP answered that jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the petition, is not lost when the petition proves meritless, and extends to Congress because the Constitution's grave abuse clause covers 'any branch or instrumentality of the government.' He conceded that where a petition shows only a breach of internal rules the Court may indeed dismiss for want of jurisdiction, and he reproduced the Separate Opinions of Justice Jose C. Vitug, who urged judicial statesmanship rather than judicial tyranny and said only a clear disregard of a specific constitutional precept can unbolt the door to intervention, and of Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero, who reaffirmed her position in Arroyo v. De Venecia. Neither, he noted, addressed jurisdiction -- and had the majority followed Mendoza, the Court would have announced that it will never review internal legislative acts, however grave the allegations.
